payload.alternatives: [{"option": "A signed 'seen' event in the record", "reason": "a format change, and a per-person reading fact sent to every clone"}, {"option": "Only count the agent-accepted rules", "reason": "the person cannot tell which of them are new to them"}]
payload.rationale: "Seen" is a fact about one person on one machine, not about the work, so it does not belong in a record every clone receives, and keeping it out changes no format. It is not destructive: the acceptance itself is signed and permanent in the record whatever happens to this file; losing the file only makes mnema show the list again. Copying it in the backup answers the maintainer's question about persistence.
payload.title: Whether the person has seen a rule an agent accepted is kept in a file of this machine, outside the record, and fails safe: a lost or unreadable file shows every agent-accepted rule again as not yet seen and never hides one; the signed accept (who, which agent, when) stays in the record, and mnema backup copies the file so a restore brings it back

payload.alternatives: [{"option": "A second reviewer account", "reason": "theatre without a second person"}, {"option": "Only document, no badge", "reason": "leaves the cheap, verifiable signal unused"}]
payload.rationale: A second reviewing account is only honest if another person really reviews; there is none. The badge is cheap and is the maintainer's own form; saying how review works is truer than a score.
payload.title: For the Scorecard's branch-protection, CODEOWNERS and code-review checks with a single maintainer: the maintainer applies for the OpenSSF Best Practices badge, and SECURITY or CONTRIBUTING says plainly that review is by one maintainer and how outside pull requests are checked

payload.alternatives: [{"option": "Raise the floor to 3.10", "reason": "a reviewer with only the Python Apple ships would have to install one to verify, breaking the verifier's promise"}, {"option": "Keep mypy pinned at 1.19.1 on 3.9", "reason": "freezes the checker on an end-of-life interpreter for no gain"}]
payload.rationale: "Python 3.9 or later, nothing to install" is the verifier's public promise, and macOS still ships Python 3.9.6 with the Command Line Tools (seen on macOS Tahoe 26.5.2 with Xcode 26.6; Apple says users cannot update it), so a reviewer on a Mac verifies without installing anything. mypy 1.20 dropped running on 3.9 but still type-checks code for 3.9 when run on 3.10+; mypy 2.0 drops that, so 2.0 waits for the floor. The floor rises when Apple changes that Python or when mypy 2.0 is worth the cost.
payload.title: The Python reader's floor stays 3.9: its tests keep running on 3.9, mypy runs on a current Python with --python-version 3.9 (so it can move to 1.20.x), and Dependabot ignores mypy 2.0 and later until the floor rises

fields.note: The maintainer chose it after the study, when asked: "Manter 3.9, mypy novo (Recommended)".
